analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal oil and gas leases held by companies caught colluding with OPEC to fix prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee from July 2024 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, with 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: If the Federal Trade Commission issues a final order finding that a company holding a federal oil or gas lease coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate oil or gas prices in violation of antitrust law, the Interior Department would have to cancel that company's federal leases, refuse to renew or extend them, and bar the company from bidding on new federal leases. The bill targets oil and gas producers on federal land whose conduct with foreign cartels raises prices American consumers pay at the pump.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who pay gasoline and heating prices influenced by oil market conditions, would benefit if the bill deters companies from coordinating with OPEC countries to restrict supply or raise prices. Taxpayers also gain from assurance that access to publicly owned oil and gas reserves is not granted to companies found to be manipulating markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who pay gas and heating prices

how_it_helps.text: If the FTC issues a final order finding a leaseholder coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate oil or gas prices in violation of the Sherman or Clayton Act, the Interior Secretary must cancel each federal oil and gas lease that company holds, to the extent allowable by law.

A company found to have manipulated prices in coordination with OPEC countries would also be barred from renewing or extending its federal leases and from bidding on any new federal oil and gas leases starting from the date of the FTC order.
The bill names the specific OPEC countries (such as Saudi Arabia, Iran, Venezuela, and the UAE) and OPEC-plus countries (including Russia and Mexico) whose coordination would trigger the penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases that the FTC finds manipulated markets in coordination with OPEC countries would lose their leases, future lease bids, and the revenue tied to federal production. More broadly, the industry would face a new penalty for price-fixing conduct.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies with federal leases

drawbacks.text: The penalty only applies if the FTC issues a final order finding coordination with a named OPEC or OPEC-plus country in violation of the Sherman or Clayton Act — a high legal bar, so the bill's practical effect depends entirely on enforcement that may never occur.
The lease cancellations are required only 'to the extent allowable by law,' acknowledging that existing leaseholders have contractual and constitutional rights that could limit or delay cancellation.

Federal onshore and offshore leases supply only part of U.S. oil and gas production, so critics could argue the bill deters more than it directly lowers prices, and antitrust enforcement against global price coordination is typically difficult to prove.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is deterrence: companies with billions tied up in federal leases would have a strong reason never to coordinate with OPEC on prices, even if the FTC order requirement means the harshest penalty would rarely fire. The main costs fall on companies actually found to have manipulated markets, which is the point of the bill. The weaknesses are practical: the trigger is hard to meet, lease cancellation faces legal limits, and the bill does nothing about price manipulation that does not involve the named foreign countries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action before the Congress ended, so it never came to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Nanette Barragán introduced the bill on July 24, 2024, with 13 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
That was the last action ever taken on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases remain unaffected: no company's leases can be cancelled for OPEC-related price manipulation under this law, since it never became law. Consumers gained nothing from a bill that could have added a penalty for coordinating with OPEC on prices.

for.name: Rep. Nanette Barragán
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 13 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.role: Cosponsor; ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; as the committee's top Democrat he was positioned to push it but the committee never acted on it.

for.name: 13 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, Norton, Carson, Titus, Omar, Watson Coleman, and Huffman
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill at introduction; no Republicans joined.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee (Rep. Bruce Westerman, chair)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 24, 2024, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; a bill cannot be voted on unless its committee reports it or leadership schedules it.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters (the sponsor plus 13 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it; with Republicans holding the House majority and the Natural Resources chairmanship, the bill had no path to a vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with federal leases
industries.note: The bill would strip federal leases and future bidding rights from any leaseholder the FTC finds manipulated oil or gas prices in coordination with OPEC or OPEC-plus countries. Because such manipulation raises prices consumers pay, the industry's interest here runs against the public's.

industries.industry: OPEC and OPEC-plus countries (including Saudi Arabia, Russia, and Venezuela)
industries.note: The bill directly targets coordination between U.S. federal leaseholders and these 21 named countries, whose output decisions shape world oil prices.

industries.industry: Consumers of gasoline and heating fuel
industries.note: Consumers would gain from deterrence of price manipulation, though the benefit depends on the FTC actually finding and proving such coordination.
